---
title: "Practice: alcohol transformations and an amount table"
---

Allow 60–75 minutes for chemistry problems and 45 minutes for the R calculation.
The R task uses the course's synthesis teaching data as preparation for later
reporting. That dataset describes aspirin formation, not an alcohol oxidation.

## 1. Keep track of the changing carbon

Draw ethanol, ethanal and ethanoic acid. Mark the carbon that changes during
oxidation and count its C–O bond orders and C–H bonds in each structure.
Assign +1 per C–O bond order, −1 per C–H bond and zero per C–C bond.
Explain why the sequence is oxidation even when no oxygen atom is added in
the first net alcohol → aldehyde transformation.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The ethanol CH₂OH carbon has one C–O and two C–H bonds, giving −1. In ethanal,
the carbonyl carbon has C=O and C–H, giving +1. In ethanoic acid it has C=O
and C–O, giving +3. Raising the carbon oxidation state is oxidation. Removing
hydrogen can accomplish that without increasing the number of oxygen atoms;
the local bond inventory, rather than simply counting O atoms in the entire
formula, gives the useful check.
:::

## 2. Predict two oxidation products and one boundary

Draw the selected oxidation product of propan-2-ol. Why does the comparable
simple oxidation pattern not apply to 2-methylpropan-2-ol without breaking
the carbon skeleton? If the target is ethanal from ethanol, why must you
consider the possibility of ethanoic acid formation when selecting conditions?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Propan-2-ol gives propanone. Its OH-bearing carbon has a C–H bond available
for the net carbonyl-forming change. The tertiary alcohol has three C–C bonds
at that carbon and no C–H; forming C=O while keeping all three carbon groups
would overbond carbon. This does not mean a tertiary alcohol is immune to
every oxidant, because harsh conditions can cleave C–C bonds. Ethanal can
undergo further oxidation, so an aldehyde target requires appropriate
controlled conditions rather than an unspecified oxidation arrow.
:::

## 3. Draw reduction in two stages

Use propanone and a hydride equivalent delivered from a reagent such as NaBH₄.
Draw addition to carbonyl carbon with the π pair moving to oxygen. Give the
alkoxide formula and charge. Then show an explicit proton transfer from water.
Name the resulting alcohol. Explain the limit of using H:⁻ in this drawing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The H-delivering pair forms a C–H bond and the C=O pair returns to O.
The resulting `(CH₃)₂CHO⁻` is an alkoxide. Its oxygen lone pair takes H
from water while the water O–H pair returns to water oxygen, giving
propan-2-ol and OH⁻. H:⁻ is shorthand for hydride-equivalent delivery from
the reagent, not free hydride coexisting in water. Detailed boron-containing
intermediates are outside this simplified introductory scheme.
:::

## 4. What would count as evidence?

Inspect the [simulated IR comparison](figures/08-ir-redox.svg). Identify the
changes consistent with converting an alcohol to a carbonyl compound.
What other observations would you request before identifying a pure isolated
product? Could a 95% isolated yield alone establish identity or purity?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
Loss of a broad alcohol O–H absorption and appearance of a carbonyl band
support the proposed functional-group change. A full spectrum, NMR or other
appropriate identification evidence and a check of sample purity would be
useful. Isolated mass can include solvent or impurities, so a large yield
does not alone identify the compound or establish purity. The supplied
traces are schematic teaching data, not observations from an actual oxidation.
:::

## 5. R task: prepare a reaction amount table

The balanced teaching equation is salicylic acid + acetic anhydride → aspirin
+ ethanoic acid, with all coefficients one. The [shared CSV](../data/amounts.csv)
supplies reagent masses and molar masses. This is a calculation context, not
a synthesis protocol. Keep the raw data unchanged.

The amount in mol is mass in g divided by molar mass in g/mol. Divide each
reactant amount by its stoichiometric coefficient. The smallest available
reaction extent limits the maximum product amount. Here aspirin's coefficient
is one and its supplied molar mass is 180.16 g/mol.

Predict which of 10.0 and 15.0 mmol will limit a 1:1 reaction, then add this
code to your report:

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
amounts <- read_csv("data/amounts.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(amount_mol = mass_g / molar_mass_g_mol,
         amount_mmol = amount_mol * 1000,
         extent_mol = amount_mol / stoich)
knitr::kable(amounts, digits = 4)
limiting_extent_mol <- min(amounts$extent_mol)
theoretical_product_mass_g <- limiting_extent_mol * 180.16
theoretical_product_mass_g
```

Knit the report. Give the limiting reagent, theoretical product amount in mmol
and mass in g. Change a copy of the acetic anhydride input to 0.51045 g and
predict the new limiting reagent before recalculating. Do not overwrite the
original CSV to make this alternative scenario.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Numerical and chemical check"}
The supplied amounts are 0.0100 mol acid and 0.0150 mol anhydride. Salicylic
acid limits the product to 10.0 mmol, corresponding to 1.8016 g aspirin.
With 0.51045 g anhydride at 102.09 g/mol, anhydride is 5.00 mmol and limits
product to 5.00 mmol, or 0.9008 g. Comparing masses alone would be wrong
because the reagents have different molar masses. In a different balanced
reaction, coefficients other than one must also be included.
:::

## Leave with

A redox transformation map, a two-stage reduction mechanism and a knitted
amount table. Continue with the [practical report guide](../reference/practical.qmd)
to distinguish theoretical yield, isolated yield, conversion and purity.
